articles.title: Conheça o Dive-LD, drone submarino dos EUA capturado pelo Irã | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo de quase 6 metros e 3 toneladas pode atingir 6 mil metros de profundidade e ser equipado para diferentes tipos de missão.
articles.summary: Veículo de quase 6 metros e 3 toneladas pode atingir 6 mil metros de profundidade e ser equipado para diferentes tipos de missão.
articles.body:
A Guarda Revolucionária do Irã afirmou nesta terça-feira (8) ter capturado um drone submarino dos Estados Unidos no Estreito de Ormuz. O equipamento foi identificado como um Dive-LD , veículo submarino autônomo desenvolvido pela empresa americana Anduril.

O modelo, avaliado em US$ 2,5 milhões (R$ 12,7 milhões, na cotação atual) , chama atenção pelo tamanho e pela capacidade de realizar missões sem a necessidade de um piloto a bordo. Ele também pode receber diferentes equipamentos e sensores, dependendo do objetivo da operação.

Mas, afinal, o que é o Dive-LD e como ele funciona?

O Dive-LD é um AUV (veículo submarino autônomo, na sigla em inglês). Diferentemente de um submarino convencional, não há pessoas dentro do equipamento.

Ele também não precisa ser controlado por um operador a todo momento. O veículo pode receber instruções sobre a missão e executar de forma autônoma tarefas de navegação e coleta de informações.

A autonomia é especialmente importante em operações submarinas, onde manter uma comunicação constante com a superfície pode ser difícil.

Dive-LD, drone subaquático dos EUA capturado pelo Irã. — Foto: Divulgação/Aduril

Apesar de ser chamado de drone, o Dive-LD está longe de ser pequeno.

O veículo tem aproximadamente 5,8 metros de comprimento e 1,2 metro de diâmetro. Dependendo da configuração, pesa cerca de 3 toneladas.

Ele foi projetado para transportar diferentes sensores e equipamentos em um espaço de mais de 1 metro cúbico.

Uma das principais características do Dive-LD é sua estrutura modular.

Isso significa que o equipamento pode ser adaptado para diferentes missões. Entre as aplicações estão:

coleta de dados sobre o ambiente submarino;

Assim, o mesmo veículo pode ser equipado de maneiras diferentes conforme o objetivo da missão.

Drone subaquático dos EUA capturado pela Guarda Revolucionária iraniana. — Foto: Reprodução

Outra característica é a profundidade que o Dive-LD consegue alcançar.

Segundo a Anduril, o veículo pode operar a até 6.000 metros abaixo da superfície.

Para isso, sua estrutura precisa suportar uma pressão enorme. Quanto maior a profundidade, maior é a pressão exercida pela água sobre o equipamento.

O Dive-LD também foi desenvolvido para permanecer muito tempo no mar.

A Anduril afirma que o veículo pode realizar missões de até 10 dias, sem precisar retornar à superfície durante esse período.

A combinação de autonomia e longa duração permite que o equipamento seja usado para monitorar grandes áreas ou realizar tarefas demoradas sem a presença constante de uma embarcação tripulada.

Apesar de atualmente fazer parte do portfólio da Anduril, o Dive-LD foi desenvolvido originalmente pela Dive Technologies, uma startup americana especializada em veículos submarinos autônomos.

A Anduril adquiriu a empresa em 2022 e incorporou o projeto ao seu conjunto de sistemas autônomos.

articles.title: Trump rebatiza lugares e promove auto-homenagens nos EUA; relembre | G1
articles.standfirst: Em menos de dois anos de segundo mandato, Trump acumulou mudanças e propostas envolvendo prédios, instituições e até acidentes geográficos, em iniciativas marcadas por auto-homenagens e disputas geopolíticas.
articles.summary: Em menos de dois anos de segundo mandato, Trump acumulou mudanças e propostas envolvendo prédios, instituições e até acidentes geográficos, em iniciativas marcadas por auto-homenagens e disputas geopolíticas.
articles.body:
Governo Trump rebatizou locais em homenagem ao presidente e em movimentos de disputa geopolítica — Foto: Montagm/g1

Desde que voltou à Casa Branca, Donald Trump transformou a mudança de nomes de lugares, prédios e instituições em uma marca de seu segundo mandato. Em menos de dois anos, o presidente dos Estados Unidos determinou novas denominações, apoiou homenagens a si próprio e propôs rebatizar locais históricos como gesto político em meio a disputas com outros países.

Algumas mudanças saíram do papel; outras esbarraram em disputas judiciais, limites legais ou na resistência de governos estrangeiros. Na mais recente ofensiva, Trump propôs trocar o nome do estado do Novo México para 'Nova América'.

Relembre abaixo as principais propostas de mudança e auto-homenagens até o momento.

Em janeiro de 2025, Donald Trump assinou uma ordem executiva para que os Estados Unidos passassem a chamar o Golfo do México de “Golfo da América ”, alegando razões de justiça e afirmando que o novo nome seria mais "bonito".

A mudança teve efeito principalmente dentro dos EUA, sem obrigar outros países a adotá-la. Google e Apple passaram a exibir a nova denominação em seus aplicativos para usuários norte-americanos.

Na época, a presidente do México, Claudia Sheinbaum, contestou a decisão e afirmou que um único país não pode determinar internacionalmente o nome da região. Em tom provocativo, ela sugeriu, ainda, que os Estados Unidos fossem rebatizados de "América Mexicana".

Em dezembro de 2025, o presidente Donald Trump propôs acrescentar o próprio nome ao Kennedy Center , histórico centro de artes cênicas de Washington criado em homenagem ao ex-presidente John F. Kennedy.

A iniciativa provocou questionamentos de congressistas, historiadores e integrantes da família Kennedy. O nome de Trump chegou a ser retirado do edifício após uma decisão judicial , mas voltou à fachada depois de uma nova decisão.

A nova inscrição, aprovada em agosto de 2026 pelo conselho do Kennedy Center, traz os dizeres: “Centro John F. Kennedy para as Artes Cênicas, restaurado e reformado pelo presidente Donald J. Trump”.

Fachada do Kennedy Center, com nome de Donald Trump inserido no início do letreiro original 'Centro Memorial John F. Kennedy de Artes Cênicas' em 19 de dezembro de 2025. — Foto: REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

Em dezembro de 2025, o nome de Donald Trump também foi acrescentado ao Instituto da Paz dos Estados Unidos. Sediada em Washington, a instituição é independente, apartidária, sem fins lucrativos e financiada pelo Congresso americano, com a missão de atuar na prevenção e resolução de conflitos violentos no exterior.

A mudança ocorreu na véspera da assinatura de um acordo de paz entre Ruanda e República Democrática do Congo, com a presença de Trump.

Ao comentar a decisão, a porta-voz da Casa Branca, Anna Kelly, afirmou que o instituto havia sido renomeado em homenagem ao presidente e disse que o novo nome serviria como um “poderoso lembrete” do que, segundo ela, uma liderança forte pode fazer pela estabilidade global.

Placa com nome do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, é fixada na frente do nome do Instituto da Paz dos EUA em Washington D.C. em 3 de dezembro de 2025. — Foto: Divulgação/Departamento de Estado dos EUA

Em julho de 2026, o aeroporto internacional de Palm Beach, na Flórida, foi rebatizado de Aeroporto Internacional Donald J. T, em mais uma homenagem ao presidente dos EUA.

A mudança foi justificada pelos fortes laços do presidente com a região. Trump é presença frequente no aeroporto porque seu luxuoso resort Mar-a-Lago fica localizado a poucos quilômetros de distância.

Placa de boas-vindas no Aeroporto Internacional de Palm Beach, que foi renomeado como "Aeroporto Internacional Presidente Donald J. Trump", em West Palm Beach, na Flórida, EUA, em 9 de julho de 2026. — Foto: Marco Bello/Reuters

Em agosto de 2026, durante a uma crise diplomática e tarifária com o Canadá, o presidente dos Estados Unidos assinou uma ordem executiva estabelecendo que o Lago Ontário passe a se chamar "Lago América". Novamente, o Google e a Apple acataram a mudança de nome em seus mapas para os estadunidenses. ‘Nova América’

➡️O Lago Ontário está entre os dois países e integra o conjunto dos cinco Grandes Lagos da América do Norte.

A decisão de Trump não obriga o Canadá a mudar o nome do lago. Autoridades canadenses rejeitaram rapidamente a ideia.

“É Lago Ontário para os canadenses e para o resto do mundo. Agora e para sempre”, escreveu o primeiro-ministro de Ontário, Doug Ford, nas redes sociais na sexta-feira.

Google Maps altera nome do Lago ontário Para Lago América — Foto: Reprodução/Google Maps

Em setembro de 2026, Trump sugeriu renomear o Estreito de Ormuz como “Estreito de Trump”, em meio à retomada dos ataques entre Estados Unidos e Irã e às disputas pelo controle da passagem.

“Agora que o temos sob controle dos EUA, deveríamos mudar o nome do Estreito de Ormuz para ESTREITO DE TRUMP???”, escreveu o presidente em sua rede social, a Truth Social.

A sugestão veio semanas depois de Trump afirmar que pretendia declarar o Estreito de Ormuz território dos Estados Unidos. O governo iraniano reagiu dizendo que a passagem está sob sua autoridade. Dias depois, Trump também compartilhou uma montagem que apresentava Ormuz como “novo território dos EUA”.

Imagem compartilhada pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, em 18 de agosto de 2026, mostra Estreito de Ormuz como 'novo território dos EUA. — Foto: Reprodução/Casa Branca no X

Também em setembro de 2026, Trump defendeu a mudança do nome do estado do Novo México para “Nova América”. Durante o feriado do Dia do Trabalho nos Estados Unidos, no dia 7, o presidente publicou memes nas redes sociais em apoio à ideia, em meio ao aumento das tensões nas negociações comerciais com o México.

Apesar das manifestações de Trump, o governo federal dos Estados Unidos não tem autoridade para alterar o nome de um estado.

O Novo México é governado pela democrata Michelle Lujan Grisham, que ocupa o cargo desde janeiro de 2019 e foi reeleita em 2022.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, em entrevista no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, em 2 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Evelyn Hockstein/ Reuters

articles.title: Mulher diz ter sido ameaçada por médium após denunciar fraudes em cartas psicografadas | G1
articles.standfirst: Os relatos fazem parte das denúncias contra a médium Mayra Rocha, em Brasília. A reportagem a procurou diversas vezes para que ela respondesse às acusações de fraude, mas ela não aceitou gravar entrevista.
articles.summary: Os relatos fazem parte das denúncias contra a médium Mayra Rocha, em Brasília. A reportagem a procurou diversas vezes para que ela respondesse às acusações de fraude, mas ela não aceitou gravar entrevista.
articles.body:
Famílias que passaram a questionar a autenticidade de cartas psicografadas atribuídas a parentes mortos afirmam ter sido ameaçadas depois de relatarem as supostas irregularidades.

Os relatos fazem parte das denúncias contra a médium Mayra Rocha, em Brasília . Segundo as famílias, o medo de retaliações fez com que algumas pessoas desistissem de denunciar.

Uma das pessoas ouvidas pela reportagem afirma ter sido ameaçada depois de questionar o conteúdo das cartas. Segundo ela, Mayra teria dito que faria uma transmissão ao vivo para revelar informações pessoais que haviam sido compartilhadas em uma conversa particular.

A situação, segundo a vítima, envolvia uma experiência pessoal dolorosa que ela havia contado à médium em um momento de confiança.

“Ela falou comigo, se eu continuasse, que ia fazer uma live, onde ela ia contar determinadas coisas que eu tinha contado para ela”, relatou Marcela Magalhães, comerciante.

Questionamentos viraram motivo de conflito

A própria Mayra deixa claro em declarações públicas que não aceita questionamentos.

"Se a pessoa for lá dizer que eu peguei na internet, até eu posso completar o recado. Agora se ela vai gostar é, de ser dito isso em público, eu não sei, né? Eu prefiro responder um processo cível, porque provavelmente vai acontecer, já que eu vou falar o nome das pessoas, prefiro pagar, né? Prefiro pagar a indenização."

Marcela Magalhães, vulnerável pela dor de perder o filho Henrique, de 18 anos, relata como se sentia ao buscar ajuda : "É tanta dor, é tanta dor que você, você acredita em qualquer coisa."

Ela relata que recebeu dois recados de seu filho Henrique durante uma transmissão ao vivo realizada por Máira Rocha. Na live, Máira mencionou o jovem : "Eu eu tô com o Henrique, um jogador de futebol que desencarnou muito cedo, mas mãezinha, ele tá bem."

No entanto, Henrique nunca foi jogador de futebol profissional, fato que alertou o marido de Marcela : "Meu marido virou pra mim e falou assim: mas ele não é jogador de futebol. Pra mim foi um erro, dela."

Marcela mais tarde identificou a origem do erro: uma fotografia de Henrique vestindo um uniforme esportivo que estava vinculada a uma reportagem de jornal sobre seu acidente de carro. A reportagem original havia cometido o mesmo erro ao descrever Henrique como jogador de futebol.

Um segundo recado de Máira gerou ainda mais desconfiança, ao associar Henrique a outras duas pessoas no carro. A médium errou ao assumir que os amigos que apareciam na foto estavam envolvidos no acidente de carro.

A imagem na realidade era uma montagem de uma campanha de alimentos realizada durante a pandemia, reunindo fotografias de três jovens que faleceram em épocas e circunstâncias distintas como uma homenagem de Marcela em suas redes. "O Henrique morreu de acidente em fevereiro de 2020. O João morreu de AVC em abril de 2020, e a Letícia morreu de um mal súbito, em 2005."

A reportagem mostra que há registros policiais contra Mayra em pelo menos cinco estados. As acusações mencionadas incluem estelionato, calúnia, difamação e ameaça.

O Ministério Público também recebeu acusações relacionadas a apropriação indébita, desvio de recursos e suposta rede de influência com servidores públicos.

As famílias afirmam que outras pessoas teriam desistido de procurar as autoridades por medo de sofrer ameaças.

articles.title: ‘Will die rather than be called a coward’: UP judge who awarded death to 23 claims death threats
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Muzaffarnagar additional district and sessions judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar, who Monday handed the death penalty to a man for burning his wife al.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Muzaffarnagar additional district and sessions judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar, who Monday handed the death penalty to a man for burning his wife alive, made disclosures about receiving death threats from gangsters in his sentencing order.The judge also referred to withdrawal of case files from his court, alleging that it was done to “save mafias and criminals”.He declared that he would not be cowed by pressure or threats. “I would rather die than be called a cowardly judge,” he recorded in his order.A total of 97 pending files involving murder and other serious cases were recalled from Diwakar’s court after it emerged in Aug that he had awarded the death sentence to 22 convicts in 10 cases over four months.An unfazed Diwakar delivered the 23rd capital punishment to Nadeem for the murder of his 23-year-old wife Shahzadi in 2018.However, in his 38-page order, he said a gangster had sent him a threatening message through an intermediary after the case files were recalled from his court.According to the judge, the message conveyed to him was: “So far, only files have been removed. If you come after us or make any comment, we will use our influence to get the court changed or get you transferred out of the district.”He alleged that some powerful gangsters in western UP enjoyed caste and political patronage and had networks extending to “higher levels”. Diwakar recorded that if he began fearing “mafia, strongmen or criminals”, it would be more appropriate for him to resign from the judicial institution.The comments acquire significance in view of Diwakar’s judicial background. Serving as Varanasi civil judge in 2022, he had ordered a videographic survey of the Gyanvapi premises.In Monday’s order, he mentioned the Gyanvapi case and said he and his family had received several death threats after that. articles.summary: Middle East News: The Middle East remains on edge on Wednesday as the United States and Iran trade fresh attacks overnight strikes. The US launched strikes on Iranian t.
articles.body: The Middle East remains on edge on Wednesday as the United States and Iran trade fresh attacks overnight strikes. The US launched strikes on Iranian targets, describing them as a response to Tehran’s attempt to target a US warship with ballistic missiles, and Iran hit back by attacking 20 vessels, including two American ships.Click here for live updatesIran, meanwhile, fired a barrage of missiles at US military positions in Jordan in direct retaliation for attacks on Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island and the port of Jask.However, Jordan said it successfully intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles launched by Iran.Here are the latest developments:CENTCOM destroys five Iranian crude oil carriers; Iran strikes backUS Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, struck and destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Tuesday, following attacks targeting a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the past two days.Four of the vessels were struck in the Gulf of Oman and were identified by CENTCOM as M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco. The fifth tanker was hit near the oil-rich Kharg Island.According to the US military, its forces ordered the crews to abandon the vessels before carrying out the strikes, rendering the tankers inoperable. No American personnel were injured in the operations.Iranian media later reported that the IRGC Navy retaliated by attacking 20 vessels, including two US ships. Ten of the vessels, including the two US ships, were reportedly targeted in the Persian Gulf, while the other 10 were struck near the Strait of Hormuz.Iran targets US Al-Azraq air base in JordanIran launched a barrage of missiles at the US air base of Al-Azraq in Jordan in what it called a "direct retaliation" for attacks on Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island and the port of Jask.According to IRIB, the initial US attack targeted an Iranian oil tanker near the Kharg Island anchorage, prompting the safe evacuation of its crew. Moments later, US forces reportedly carried out a second strike on a commercial vessel in the coastal waters off Jask County. Another explosion of unidentified origin was also reported in the area.Amid the escalating hostilities, the Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy issued an urgent evacuation warning.The IRGC later vowed to retaliate by targeting oil tankers near ports in Bahrain and Kuwait.Iranian Navy claims US submarine captureThe IRGC Navy on Tuesday claimed that it had captured a US unmanned submersible near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz during what it described as a "complex intelligence" and operational operation.Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that IRGC Navy forces “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, unmanned submarines” operated by the US military in the early hours of Tuesday.The submersible was reportedly equipped with advanced underwater technology and had been delivered to the US fleet in 2025.Iran’s state news agency IRNA described the vessel as being equipped with some of the world’s most advanced underwater technology and called it a “war trophy”.IRNA also reported that photographs of the captured submersible were expected to be released in the coming hours.The United States has yet to publicly comment on the IRGC Navy’s claim.Separately, a US Central Command official confirmed that an American underwater drone had “malfunctioned and gone missing a day ago” and was no longer in the command’s possession.CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the Anduril Dive-LD drone went missing while conducting a survey mission in the region.Hawkins said the vessel was an older, defective model that “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”.“It was also in a commercially available configuration, so we aren't concerned,” Hawkins added.US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran, targets aviation industryThe Trump administration on Tuesday (local time) imposed fresh sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers in a renewed effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.The measures are part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast” campaign, aimed at cutting off what it described as “critical financial lifelines” to Iran’s already heavily sanctioned government. The latest sanctions target remaining parts of Tehran’s beleaguered aviation network, which has faced years of restrictions from Washington.“Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system,” a statement quoted treasury secretary Scott Bessent as saying.The administration accused the 36 entities targeted in the latest round of sanctions of supporting Iran’s efforts to use its aviation sector to transport weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.It also alleged that private companies in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia provided parts and logistical support to Mahan Air. The airline has been under US counterterrorism sanctions since 2019 over its alleged support for Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which the State Department has designated a foreign terrorist organisation.(With agency inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More delays expected across UK after air traffic glitch cancels over 1,000 flights
articles.summary: UK News: Flight delays are expected to continue across the UK on Wednesday after an air traffic control glitch cancelled more than 1,000 flights and disrupted .
articles.body: Flight delays are expected to continue across the UK on Wednesday after an air traffic control glitch cancelled more than 1,000 flights and disrupted the journeys of tens of thousands of passengers.The disruption was caused by a fault in the flight data processing system operated by National Air Traffic Services, which manages flight plans and other operational information used by air traffic controllers.Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe said there would be a full investigation into what went wrong. He said resolving the problem had taken "longer than hoped".Airlines and airports warned that disruption could continue even after the technical fault was resolved because of the backlog of flights.Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed by up to eight hours on Tuesday.At Heathrow, departures were initially paused around lunchtime before operations resumed and then faced further disruption in the afternoon.The airport is understood to have run out of space for incoming aircraft because planes were unable to depart. Thirteen Heathrow-bound flights were diverted to airports in the UK and Europe.According to FlightRadar, Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham were among the worst-affected airports.UK transport secretary Heidi Alexander said it would take time for flight operations to fully recover and urged passengers to check with their airlines before travelling. She also said she was seeking assurances that lessons would be learned and aviation systems were "up to the job".Airports affected included London Stansted and London City, along with Manchester, Birmingham, Gatwick and airports in Scotland. articles.title: Tung Chee-hwa: Hong Kong's first leader after British handover to China dies
articles.summary: The tenure of Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after Britain handed over the city to China, was marked by crises and protests.
articles.body:
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89.

The former shipping scion took over the reins from the last British Governor Chris Patten in July 1997 when the UK handed Hong Kong back to China , ending more than 150 years of British control.

Tung's rocky tenure was marked by the Asian Financial Crisis, two major epidemics, and historic protests which attracted criticism of his administration. He eventually resigned in 2005.

Tung died on Tuesday night surrounded by loved ones, local media reported. His office described him as a man "devoted to his country and its people".

Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from Liverpool University in the UK before moving to the US, where he worked at General Electric for almost a decade.

In 1969, he moved to Hong Kong and worked in his father's shipping conglomerate, the Orient Overseas, eventually taking over the reins in 1979.

His political career began in 1992 when he was appointed a member of Patten's executive council.

Despite having little political experience, Tung was believed to be handpicked by Beijing to lead Hong Kong after the handover. He was seen as a loyalist, especially after China's state-run banks helped rescue his family business during a global slump in the mid-1980s.

During a reception at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996, China's then-president Jiang Zemin walked across a packed room to shake Tung's hands – a widely photographed gesture that at the time famously signalled Beijing's backing of Tung for the top job.

The Asian Financial Crisis hit shortly after Tung took over, which sent home prices diving. His administration was also beset by a series of public health challenges, including a bird flu outbreak from 1997 to 2002 and the 2003 outbreak of Sars, also known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome.

But Tung's biggest political challenge took place in July 2003 during his second term, when half a million Hongkongers took to the streets to protest against a proposed national security law they feared would threaten their civic rights.

His administration abandoned the proposed legislation following the massive outcry, which also contributed to Tung stepping down in March 2005.

At the time his declining health was cited as a reason - but some said he was pressured by Beijing to step down.

Beijing ultimately imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which authorities have argued is necessary to maintain stability. Critics however have called it "the end of Hong Kong" and say it has created a climate of fear in the city.

Tung's last public outing was in July 2021, at an event marking the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. He underwent heart surgery months later, according to reports.

He is survived by his wife and three children.

Hong Kong's former chief executives have paid tribute to Tung. Leung Chun-ying, who led the city between 2012 and 2017, described him as a "benevolent" leader who "won people over with reason".

Carrie Lam, who was the chief executive from 2017 to 2022, said Tung's leadership made "a historic contribution with lasting benefits".

China's state news agency Xinhua called Tung a "renowned patriot, distinguished social activist, close friend of the Communist Party of China".

It also noted that Tung had served as one of many vice-chairmen of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body, for four consecutive terms.

articles.title: 18-year-old Arpit Jai lost his life in Delhi’s Satya Niketan PG collapse; what his parents did next has given his tragedy a new meaning: “He cant be here but…”
articles.summary: For Arpit Jai’s family, Sunday began like an ordinary day. By the end of it, their 18-year-old son was gone. Arpit Jai had just returned to Delhi afte.
articles.body: For Arpit Jai’s family, Sunday began like an ordinary day. By the end of it, their 18-year-old son was gone. Arpit Jai had just returned to Delhi after spending the Rakshabandhan holidays with his family in Dewas, Madhya Pradesh. He reached his PG accommodation in Satya Niketan on Sunday morning. Hours later, the five-storey building came crashing down, trapping students beneath the rubble. Arpit was among those who did not make it out alive.In the middle of a loss that is difficult to put into words, his family has made a decision that could allow a part of their son to live on: they donated his corneas.Arpit was a second-year student at Delhi University’s Atma Ram Sanatan Dharam College and was among the seven people killed in the Satya Niketan PG building collapse. The family chose to donate his corneas even as they struggled to come to terms with his death.He had only just returned to DelhiArpit reached Delhi at around 7 am on Sunday after spending Rakshabandhan at his home in Dewas, MP. By afternoon, the building where he was staying, identified as Hostel Daze, had collapsed. His family tried calling him after learning about the collapse, but his phone was switched off. His parents then left for Delhi. Later, the search ended with the worst possible news.Arpit’s father, Bhupendra Jai, later described the shock. “My son had just returned from our hometown after the Rakshabandhan holidays. He had reached back to his PG yesterday morning, and the next time we saw is his dead body,” he said as per various media reports.The grief was accompanied by regret. His father said the family had not known about the condition of the accommodation. “Everyone is telling us how bad the condition of the PG. I wish my son had told me before. I would have never let him stay there,” he said.A night of searching, then a painful identificationFor Arpit’s friends and family, the hours after the collapse were spent searching for him. One of Arpit’s friends told media outlets that they had been looking for Arpit through the night. Eventually, AIIMS informed them that a body matched the identity details they had provided.Arpit’s family was eventually able to confirm his identity through birthmarks. “At around 6:30 am, his family reached, and finally they were able to do the identification of Arpit. The mother confirmed it by birthmarks on his body,” the friend said.In the middle of grief, a decision to giveThere was little that could make the loss easier. Arpit was young, had returned from home only hours earlier and had been looking forward to going back to college. Despite the shock, amid that grief, Arpit’s family agreed to donate his corneas.According to Official Humans of Bombay, Arpit’s father looked at his son one last time and said “My boy had so much left to see,” he said. “If he can’t be here, let his eyes help someone else see.” Before leaving for Arpit’s last rites, the family donated his corneas at AIIMS.Seven lives lost in the Satya Niketan collapseArpit was one of seven people killed when the PG building in Satya Niketan collapsed on Sunday afternoon. The building, known as Hostel Daze, was being used as accommodation for students near Delhi University's South Campus. Rescue teams pulled 12 people from the debris, while seven died.Police said repair or construction work was underway when the structure collapsed. The building's owner, Hariram Gupta, was later arrested in Rajasthan's Bhiwadi area. A magisterial inquiry was also ordered into the incident.The collapse has since raised wider questions about student accommodation in the area, including the condition of old buildings, unauthorised construction and safety arrangements in privately operated PGs. Students living in nearby accommodations began leaving the area after the incident, with some parents asking their children to return home.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.body: The recent building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan PG has once again raised the uncomfortable question Delhi has been grappling with: what happens when old structures become unsafe?Continuing to live in an ageing building can be a matter of life and death, but tearing them down and rebuilding them can be an expensive proposition, one not everyone can afford.That is about to change under Delhi’s proposed new Master Plan, which is betting on higher Floor Area Ratio (FAR) to make redevelopment a more viable proposition for property owners.The higher FAR could give owners of aging buildings additional development potential, providing them with a financial reason to tear down old structures and rebuild them while helping offset the cost of demolition.D Thara, secretary, department of capital development, ministry of housing and urban affairs, said the provision assumes significance as Delhi grapples with old buildings, particularly after the recent collapse of a five-storey paying guest accommodation in Satya Niketan that killed seven people.More construction potential for old buildingsThara said the proposed plan has given considerable room for regeneration and redevelopment, including additional FAR for old properties.“In the master plan, we have proposed regeneration and redevelopment. We have also given FAR. If the building is old, we need money to demolish it. For that, you need extra FAR. That has been given in the master plan this time,” Thara said on the sidelines of the National Conference on Real Estate for Viksit Bharat: Enabling Growth, Investment & Ease of Doing Business, organised by ASSOCHAM.Explaining the extent of the additional development potential, she said most old buildings currently have a FAR of 1.5.“Most of these old buildings are 1.5 FAR. If we demolish it, they will get 50 per cent more,” she said.Thara said the additional FAR could help deal with the financial burden involved in demolishing and reconstructing ageing properties.“I cannot give a response to the city level issues here. I am talking from the government of India. But, for regeneration and redevelopment, we have given a lot of scope this time,” she said.The proposed approach comes as Delhi faces the twin challenges of addressing ageing structures and providing more housing and urban infrastructure.Metro corridors to drive high-density developmentThe Master Plan also envisages a substantial expansion in housing, with up to 40 lakh new homes potentially coming up in Delhi over the next 20 years, according to Thara.Around 20,000 hectares along Metro corridors have been identified for high-density development. The idea is to encourage housing and commercial activity around areas that are connected by public transport.“We want densities on the metro corridor. We want densities where people don’t need to use cars. So, it’s high time we bring the people to the metro corridors,” she said.Thara referred to a survey which, according to her, showed that around 70 per cent of jobs are located around Metro corridors. She also pointed to Delhi’s substantial road network and high road density, stressing the need to make better use of existing infrastructure.‘Sponge cities’ approach to rainfallThe proposed urban development framework also touches on how Delhi manages rainwater and waterlogging.Thara called for cities to change the way they handle rainfall, particularly as extreme weather events become more frequent. She advocated the concept of “sponge cities”, where urban areas absorb and retain rainwater rather than allowing large volumes of it to quickly enter drainage systems.“The new concept is sponge cities. Absorb the water, rather than letting it go,” she said.She also questioned construction practices that prevent rainwater from reaching the ground, urging real estate developers and individual property owners to examine how they build and pave their properties.“When we construct our houses independently also, do we look at what do we do? We lay concrete to stop water (from absorbing in the soil). The water that used to go there, where will it go?” she said.Land pooling needs landowners’ confidenceThara also spoke about land pooling, saying the first scheme had been approved but that the participation of landowners would be important for the process to advance.“Land pooling will only move forward when people have faith. This is the first step. The second step is to come together as an association,” she said.She said the DDA would have to play a greater role in land aggregation. A platform is also being created to facilitate interaction between individual landowners and the authority.The proposals come against the backdrop of concerns over ageing buildings in Delhi, alongside the need to accommodate future housing and urban development. The Satya Niketan collapse has brought renewed focus on old structures, while the proposed higher FAR is intended to provide greater development potential for regeneration and redevelopment.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: MCD begins demolition of building next to collapsed Satya Niketan PG that killed 7
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi on Tuesday began the controlled demolition of a building adjoining the structure that collapsed in south.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi on Tuesday began the controlled demolition of a building adjoining the structure that collapsed in south Delhi's Satya Niketan on September 6, killing at least seven people and injuring five.An MCD official said the adjoining building had been declared dangerous and the demolition exercise was stopped in the evening. Work will resume on Wednesday morning, the official added.The building had housed a girls' paying guest accommodation and was evacuated after the neighbouring five-storey structure collapsed on Sunday.The MCD had issued an order on the day of the collapse directing the owner or occupier of property No. 13 in Satya Niketan to demolish the structure, citing the danger it posed to residents and neighbouring buildings.Officials had earlier said that the students staying in the building had already vacated it and were returning only to collect their belongings before the demolition.Meanwhile, concerns over unsafe and tilting buildings have also emerged in north Delhi's Nehru Vihar, where residents alleged that a building had tilted several times over nearly a decade because of a faulty sewer line.According to a resident, the structure was demolished and rebuilt once, but developed the same problem again within a few years. The building, which is less than eight years old, was most recently reconstructed around three years ago.Residents alleged that repeated complaints to civic agencies had gone unheard and claimed that poor maintenance by authorities, including the Delhi Jal Board and the MCD, had contributed to the problem.One resident alleged that at least 400 dwellings in the nearby F Block of Gandhi Vihar were tilting in one direction or another. articles.title: Delhi building collapse: PG operator Sudhanshu arrested
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Wednesday arrested PG operator Sudhanshu in connection with the Satya Niketan building collapse that left seven people dead.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Wednesday arrested PG operator Sudhanshu in connection with the Satya Niketan building collapse that left seven people dead.Police had earlier arrested alleged owner Hariram Gupta, his wife Urmila and their son Mahesh.According to investigators, the property was registered in Urmila's name, the electricity connection was in Hariram's name, while Mahesh was involved in managing the PG.Also read: 4 floors higher, Rs 4 lakh a month: The greed behind Delhi PG ‘Hostel Daze’Rescue operation ends after 27 hoursThe five-storey building housing the boys' PG near Delhi University's South Campus collapsed around 1.30pm on Sunday.After more than 27 hours of rescue work, the operation ended at 5.10pm on Monday, with officials confirming that all debris had been cleared. A total of 12 people were rescued, seven of whom died.Rescuers repeatedly switched between heavy machinery and manual excavation while searching for survivors. Oxygen cylinders were also lowered into cavities to help those trapped breathe.Family's role, renovation work under probeHariram was initially untraceable after the collapse and was later apprehended in Bhiwadi. Police had formed 10 teams to trace him and also issued a Look Out Circular.Police subsequently arrested Urmila and Mahesh. Investigators are examining the family's role in the property and the running of the PG, besides checking whether they operated other PG facilities in the area.Police are also probing renovation work allegedly being carried out in the basement before the collapse. Locals said water had accumulated there after days of rain and claimed the work may have weakened the structure.The building, known as Hostel Daze, stood on around 55 square yards in a resettlement colony where permission had reportedly been granted only for a G+1 structure. The MCD said the building violated construction norms.Five MCD officials suspendedThe Delhi government suspended five South Zone MCD officials: deputy commissioner Rakesh Kumar, superintending engineer Ranvir Singh, executive engineer Lalit Kumar Goel, assistant engineer Sunil Chauhan and junior engineer Ashish Kumar.MCD commissioner Sanjiv Khirwar said the action followed local allegations and the ongoing inquiry into basement work, while asserting that the civic body had “zero tolerance” towards unauthorised construction.The Delhi government has also ordered a magisterial inquiry into the collapse.Further investigation is underway.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Amazon cargo jet pilots tried to abort unstable landing before plane overran Miami runway
articles.summary: US News: Pilots of an Amazon cargo jet that overshot the runway at Miami International Airport had tried to abort an unstable landing, according to information.
articles.body: Pilots of an Amazon cargo jet that overshot the runway at Miami International Airport had tried to abort an unstable landing, according to information released by investigators on Tuesday (local time).Upon landing, the plane overshot the runway and crashed into a van, killing five people inside. The accident occurred on September 13, and the flight recorders were recovered a day later.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the crash. Investigators will interview the pilot, co-pilot and crew members on Wednesday as they seek to determine why the jet overran the runway.The crash injured five other people, two of whom remain in critical condition while a third is in stable condition. The pilot and co-pilot have since been released from hospital.Miami-Dade Sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.Did pilots hesitate?The Amazon jet was landing after a two-hour flight from Puerto Rico as storms brewed around Miami airport. According to the NTSB, the plane barrelled roughly 1,300 feet (396 metres) past the end of the runway.According to Mike O'Donnell, a former Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the fact that the plane landed on its nose and right landing gear first indicated an unstable landing. He suggested the pilot might have been attempting a “go-around” to retry the landing approach.“A go-around probably should have been executed sooner than that. And it seems like they hesitated,” he added.By the time the crew tried to abort the landing, O’Donnell noted, it may have been too late if there wasn’t enough runway left. However, interviews investigators have scheduled with the pilots for Wednesday are expected to provide more insight into what they were thinking at that moment.Aviation attorney Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, observed that “it almost seems like there was a disagreement between the pilots on what to do.”Video of the landing showed the plane hovering above the runway for a long time without flaring the nose to bring the wheels onto the ground. Experts said it appeared a strong tailwind propelled the plane far past the point where it was supposed to land. Air traffic controllers had also not changed the approach to the runway to allow the plane to land into a headwind.Meanwhile, two of the Miami airport’s four runways remained closed on Tuesday and will not reopen until NTSB investigators have gathered all the information they need from the crash site.More than 225 flights have been cancelled since Sunday, while hundreds more have been delayed.(With AP inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Drug gangs exploited and raped us as teens, then police failed us, women tell BBC
articles.summary: Four victims describe being targeted by criminals and then not being taken seriously by the authorities.
articles.body:
Warning: Contains details of sexual exploitation

Christine was 13 when she began exchanging messages online with someone she believed was a teenage boy.

On their first meeting, she discovered he was a grown man 10 years older than herself. He also told her he was involved with gangs and drugs.

"I always knew, OK, he's probably hurt someone, but in terms of hurting me, I didn't think it would get to that point," she says.

Over the next few years, he would use Christine to courier drugs, subject her to extreme sexual exploitation, and assault her so violently she feared she might die.

Christine is one of four women who have chosen to waive their anonymity and speak publicly to the BBC documentary, Britain's Forgotten Girls , about how they were targeted by criminals when they were children.

Their stories, covering 2002 to last year, differ in detail - but reveal strikingly similar patterns of abuse. All four describe being targeted by boys and older men connected to drug gangs, manipulated into abusive relationships, then repeatedly sexually exploited.

All believe the authorities failed to protect them and did not take their allegations seriously.

The sexual and criminal exploitation of girls by drug gangs has long been overshadowed in public discussion by the focus on sexual grooming gangs, according to front-line social workers and experts in the field.

"For grooming gangs, the primary purpose is often the sexual exploitation of those girls, but the primary purpose of a drug gang is to make money off selling drugs and other criminal activity," says Connie Muttock from the children's charity, Centre for Young Lives.

Girls are brought in to generate money, says Muttock, but many are also sexually abused by gang members.

A recent government audit of group-based sexual abuse and exploitation in England and Wales said that authorities often fail these victims.

The BBC understands that the issue of drug gangs will be tackled in an independent inquiry set up in response to the audit.

Christine grew up in London, but moved to Coventry with her mother after her parents' divorce. She says she felt disorientated and alone in her new home.

"In school, everybody already had their friendship groups because of how late I'd moved in," she says. "I didn't really feel like I had friends."

"We'd be texting through the night," she says.

Christine claimed to be 16 in her texts. When she eventually met the man, she admitted she was 13, but he told her that age did not matter.

"He was like, 'that doesn't change anything. I still want to be with you.' And that's when we started, like, quote unquote, going out."

The thrill of feeling wanted was also what led Annie, from south-east London, into the clutches of a gang.

At first, she says she "felt quite in awe, quite excited to have the attention" of three older boys who wanted to befriend her, even though she knew they were involved in drugs.

For both Christine and Annie, what began as attention, affection or friendship gradually turned into coercion and exploitation.

One evening, Annie says, the boys got her drunk and then repeatedly raped her, photographing the abuse.

They then threatened to share the photos if she did not agree to have "more sex, with more people".

The abuse went on for years, she says. "They would just use me. Just rape me again and again."

Christine says the abuse escalated on her 14th birthday, when her boyfriend asked her to sleep with his friends to "help him out".

"And I did it. I felt disgusting, but he made it out like it was something he really needed."

After that, "it became an expectation" that she would sleep with other men.

The sexual and physical abuse continued for more than eight years, says Christine, as she was repeatedly raped by men connected to her boyfriend's drug gang.

Rape, and the pimping out of girls, is common in the violent and hyper-masculine environment of drug gangs, says Muttock.

"As long as we've had drug gangs in [the UK] we have had girls being abused and coerced within them."

Holly, from Manchester, describes how she was not only abused sexually, but also exploited criminally.

Recruited by a gang as a child, she sold drugs in the city centre, she says, and later delivered them to locations across the UK, as far away as Carlisle and London.

One of the reasons gangs criminally exploit girls is - according to the National Crime Agency - "due to their belief that women are less likely to be suspected of, or stopped and searched for, dealing drugs".

Holly says she was also sexually assaulted numerous times by members of the gang: "After a while it just became normal to me."

She convinced herself it meant she was wanted, and part of a family that cared for her.

These patterns of abuse were identified in a 2012 report, although those involved say that it failed to generate the response it deserved.

The Children's Commission for England carried out an inquiry into sexual exploitation of children in gangs and groups , and suggested an estimated 16,500 were at risk of abuse from grooming groups or criminal gangs.

"Some people, including people in senior positions... found it very difficult to accept the real scale of what was going on," recalls the then-deputy Children's Commissioner for England, Sue Berelowitz, who headed the inquiry.

One senior government source was quoted by the BBC as saying the report's language was "hysterical".

Publication also coincided with the conviction of nine Asian men for grooming young girls for sex in Rochdale.

Headlines about sexual grooming - a serious but distinct issue - "complicated things", according to Prof Carlene Firmin of Durham University, who carried out some research for the 2012 inquiry.

Ministers in the government accused the inquiry report of downplaying the role of Asian abusers, but Berelowitz said the evidence showed the abuse crossed every cultural and ethnic group.

All four women who have spoken to us they believe their plight was not taken seriously by police.

When Christine was 15, social services alerted police to her case, but she says investigators were more interested in the drug offences committed by gang members than the abuse she was reporting.

"I sat for hours and hours in interviews... but the moment I told them about the drugs and the houses, everything shifted," she says - detectives wanted more information about the drug dealing.

"Little old me coming and saying, 'this is the abuse I'm going through', wasn't enough."

Another woman, Violet, who became involved with a south London drug gang when she was 13, tells a similar story.

She reported that she had been repeatedly raped and sexually abused by gang members, she says.

The men were arrested on drugs offences. But Violet says when she later asked about the progress of the rape investigation, she was told that police officers had "bigger fish to fry".

She eventually received statutory compensation from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, but learned by letter that her case had been closed without going to court.

The experience was "pretty shocking, pretty offensive, pretty insensitive", she says.

Holly recalls approaching police as she fled a sexual assault, covered in cuts and bruises. She says an officer accused her of just trying to get a "free lift home" in a police car.

Meanwhile, Annie was informed her attackers would not be prosecuted because there was no realistic chance of a conviction.

"I felt the fact [the police] did nothing really made me feel like it wasn't abuse," she says. "It made me feel like it was my fault."

None of the women interviewed by the BBC have ever seen anyone prosecuted for the abuse they say they suffered.

In the 2025 audit, Baroness Louise Casey was asked by the government to establish the scale of group-based child sexual abuse offending in England and Wales.

The issue of girls exploited by drug gangs did not form a significant part of her report, although it expressed concerns that authorities were failing to spot when a child was being both criminally and sexually exploited.

The then-home secretary Yvette Cooper drew attention to the subject in parliament, saying: "I do not believe that this kind of exploitation has been sufficiently investigated."

The BBC understands the issue of sexual and criminal exploitation by drug gangs in England and Wales will now be examined by the Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs, established by the government in response to Baroness Casey's report.

Speaking on behalf of the National Police Chiefs' Council, Acting Chief Constable Rebecca Riggs described the experiences of the women as "devastating" and said she was "deeply sorry" if people felt they were not listened to, believed, or given the response they needed.

"We did not always get it right, and where we failed victims, we continue to acknowledge it and learn from it," she told the BBC.

Teenage girls lured into forced sex by gangs in London, BBC finds

Today, Violet, Holly, Annie and Christine have managed to rebuild their lives.

Violet works in reproductive health services, while Annie runs Hear Her Collective, which seeks to improve support for girls and young women.

Holly now researches child criminal exploitation and the care system at the University of Sheffield. She says she is happy to have found a job where she can talk openly about the ordeal of her teenage years.

For Christine, who recently graduated from university and got married, talking about the past is also important.

She has written and published a book based on her own experiences.

"I've learned to turn my pain into purpose," she says. "It's not been an easy journey."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line

articles.title: Wolverhampton Art Gallery wins £100,000 award for youth projects
articles.summary: The gallery is one of three winners of the inaugural Freelands Awards.
articles.body:
Wolverhampton Art Gallery has been awarded £100,000 to develop more opportunities for young people.

The cultural venue is one of three winners of the inaugural Freelands Awards, which recognise organisations with "progressive art education approaches with demonstrable impact".

The gallery was recognised for two projects within its arts and cultures youth programme, which provide free support for young people to develop their creative skills and careers.

ArtForum is a free, hands-on group for 14 to 25-year-olds, while MORE ART INC is aimed at emerging artists, aged 16 to 30, from the city and its surrounding areas.

Stephen Simkins, leader of the City of Wolverhampton Council, which owns the gallery, said the award was a "fantastic endorsement" of the gallery's work with young people.

"The art gallery youth programmes have created opportunities for young people from across the city, some who didn't think that art galleries were somewhere they belonged but have now gone on to start inspiring careers in the creative industries," he said.

The Freelands Awards were established by the Freelands Foundation, which said visual arts organisations gave important opportunities for lifelong teaching and learning, despite declining funding and rising operating costs.

The winners were chosen by a panel of judges who reviewed entries from arts organisations across the UK, before visiting those shortlisted.

The three winners will now work with the Freelands Foundation to create case study films about their programmes, which will be shared as resources for other organisations.

articles.title: How Kielder Water protects the North East from drought
articles.summary: How did England's least populated region become home to its largest, drought-battling reservoir?
articles.body:
Much of England has faced drought conditions during a summer marked by repeated heatwaves, but the North East has been spared water scarcity despite experiencing what the Environment Agency dubs "prolonged dry weather".

One of the, quite literally, biggest reasons is that Northumberland is home to England's largest reservoir – Kielder Water.

So how did the country's least populated region gain this huge asset and will the lake continue to protect the North East from water shortages long into the future?

Kielder Water opened in 1982 and is the biggest man-made lake in the UK, holding about 200bn litres of water.

Jonty Hall, then aged nine, was chosen to press the button to start filling the reservoir, flooding the multiple farms and homes that once stood on the dry site.

"This is now my 37th year," he said, referring to his work for Northumbrian Water at the lake he helped create.

The reservoir had been built with the expectation that the area's water-hungry steel industry would continue to expand, but the predicted boom never lasted.

Instead, Kielder Water now plays a part in ensuring the North East is one of the "most water secure regions" in the world, according to Newcastle University hydrology researcher Dr Anna Murgatroyd.

Right now, water from Kielder is being used to top up the River Wear to maintain minimum levels.

The Department for Environment, Food and Environment said about 560 Olympic-sized swimming pools worth of water had been diverted from Kielder to the Wear since mid-July, and the lake can be similarly used to protect the likes of the Tyne, Tees and Derwent.

But Kielder is not the only reason the region is relatively protected from droughts today, said Murgatroyd.

The region is home to numerous other reservoirs and enjoys relatively high rainfall.

Its large river systems also provide locals with a "good amount of water".

While Kielder continues to give the North East a high level of protection, the effects of climate change have led to questions about the region's future water security.

Murgatroyd was part of a team that modelled climate effects across England and Wales up to 2080, work that suggested the North East would see a rise in drought conditions but remain more water secure than other regions.

Prof Kiran Tota-Maharaj, from the University of Hull, said Kielder remains an example of "best practice" in water engineering.

"It has served its purpose and it is resilient, especially during unforeseen conditions," he said.

But he warned climate change was changing weather patterns so much that "predictability was becoming more and more challenging".

Northumbrian Water, which has no current plans to build new reservoirs, said its estimates suggested the North East would have enough water to meet demand for the foreseeable future.

But it said this did not mean the region possessed unlimited resources, so it was encouraging people to be more considerate in their water use.

"Kielder is a major safeguard," a spokesperson said, "but saving water reduces pressure on the whole supply system and environment and makes that safeguard last longer."

articles.title: Home heating oil: 'We were target of sinister theft and want to warn others'
articles.summary: A charity is warning about the risk of home heating oil thefts after falling victim to the crime.
articles.body:
The head of a rural community charity has warned of the growing risk of home heating oil theft after her own organisation fell victim to thieves.

Kate Clifford, director of the Rural Community Network (RCN), arrived at the charity's offices one morning to find the heat was not working.

"We initially thought there must be a leak, but then we could see damage to the tank and knew something was seriously wrong," she said.

The charity had only recently filled its tank with more than 1,000 litres of oil which police later confirmed had been stolen.

Clifford said: "The tank at our offices isn't easily accessible, and somebody must have known we had recently filled up, so the worrying thing was it felt very premediated, and that felt quite sinister.

"We are a charity, so we have to be very careful with our funds, so to lose this was a huge expense to us and then we had to spend money on extra security measures."

The theft at the charity's Cookstown offices happened in 2024, but the charity is speaking out as new figures show there have been 600 reports of oil and fuel thefts in Northern Ireland since 2021.

Home heating oil is a key energy source for heating and hot water in the majority of households across Northern Ireland.

The Consumer Council for Northern Ireland said its tends to get more reports of oil thefts during an energy crisis when the price of oil is often pushed up because of geopolitics and global events.

Police figures show that oil thefts in Northern Ireland peaked around Russia's invasion of Ukraine and have been fluctuating ever since.

So far this year, there has been a small increase in oil and fuels thefts in the first six months of 2026, which saw oil prices impacted by the US-Israel war with Iran.

From January to June, there were 45 oil thefts in Northern Ireland compared to 59 during the whole of last year.

In March, BBC News NI spoke to a family from Limavady who had to move out of their home after heating oil thieves struck and turned the property into a "massive biohazard".

"In March 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, 500 litres peaked to around £663 and 900 litres peaked to around £1,182," said Raymond Gormley, head of energy policy at the Consumer Council.

"This time period corresponded with the highest number of oil thefts, with the police figures showing 37 in a single month.

"This year geopolitics in the middle east are once again affecting things and we've had contacts from families impacted by thefts, so it's definitely something people need to be aware of."

Gormley said there are a number of steps that people can take to improve security around their heating oil.

"Install a lock or alarm on your oil tank and fit hardened flexible casings to any visible fuel hoses so that they are harder to cut.

"Another thing people can do is keep your garden or drive gates closed and securely locked as well as installing security lighting which can warn you or alert a neighbour of an intruder."

In May, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) published a social media post warning the public of the dangers of oil thefts in Mid-Ulster following a number of incidents in the Moneymore area.

In July, the Consumer Council reported that the average cost of 500 litres of home heating oil jumped from £346.59 to £445.37 in the space of three weeks – an increase of £98.78 (29%).

The organisation said the price rise was in response to the recent escalation in fighting between the US and Iran.

At the beginning of September the average cost of 500 litres of oil in Northern Ireland had risen to £491.00.

Almost two-thirds of homes (62.5%) in Northern Ireland use oil for heating, the highest proportion among UK nations.

In rural parts of the country, the dependency on home heating oil rises to about 80%.

Clifford believes home heating oil theft highlights a wider inequality facing rural Northern Ireland.

"While urban households often have access to gas networks and a choice of energy suppliers many rural households depend on a single fuel source stored outside their homes," she said.

"This creates a unique vulnerability to crime that disproportionately affects rural residents, particularly older people, low-income households, and farms."

"Rural communities are often at their strongest when neighbours look out for one another, so if you notice suspicious activity, unfamiliar vehicles repeatedly visiting an area, or anyone behaving unusually around fuel tanks, report it to the PSNI."

A spokesperson for the PSNI said fuel tanks can often be seen as "easy pickings" for thieves.

"By taking precautions you can protect your oil – lock and disguise your tank, fit a 'level Gauge' with audible alarm and consider installing security lighting and CCTV."

articles.title: Billericay actor challenges pregnancy stereotypes in new film
articles.summary: Due Dating, written by and starring Jade Asha, follows the experience of dating during pregnancy.
articles.body:
An actor says she was able to draw on her own pregnancy while writing and starring in a movie about a woman taking the plunge and dating during her third trimester.

Jade Asha, 36, from Billericay, Essex, who has been acting for more than 20 years, pitched the idea for Due Dating in the early stages of her own pregnancy and then spent three months writing the screenplay.

The film, which premieres in London next month, is described as a "bold and thought-provoking romantic comedy drama".

Mother-of-two Asha, whose son made a cameo appearance at the end of the movie, said: "As an actor you're always looking for interesting and new works."

While writing the story, Asha said she felt like she had a sense of responsibility to showcase pregnancy in a candid way.

The personal journey of a pregnant woman is rarely highlighted, she said.

"Usually what you see is the happy ending - but we don't see the amazing but scary nine months," she added.

Asha said she wanted to help women feel less alone during a vulnerable time and that showing her bump was very important to her.

"It did not look like a pretty bump - mine had stretch marks and veins showing," she said.

"You're still expected to be a pretty woman."

She got the original idea for the story from a targeted ad on social media about pregnant women dating. The comments, she said, were sharp-tongued and quick to condemn dating during pregnancy, with some offering condolences to the baby's father.

"As a pregnant woman there are all these things you are not allowed to do," Asha added.

"You've got to put yourself first, without the judgement."

The story follows Cherry, played by Asha, who becomes the muse of a blogger who has to change his lifestyle and learn how to write from a woman's perspective in order to keep his job.

She said the film explored whether pregnant women really had the right to their own autonomy.

"When I first fell pregnant, it took me by surprise, I had just got married, and it was a honeymoon baby," she told the BBC.

But working on the movie alongside her own pregnancy "meant we had a deadline so we had to do it - but it was also terrifying".

Doulas, midwives and anyone who works in maternity can watch the film for free at the movie's premiere on Leicester Square at the Prince Charles Theatre on 19 October.

Asha said: "We would just really love to have the people who keep the world ticking around and don't get thanks for it or maybe not as much as they should."

articles.title: Orchestras For All helps man with autism feel he belongs
articles.summary: Since joining the group, the man has grown in confidence and is now holds a Guinness World Record.
articles.body:
A trumpet player says an accessible orchestra has helped him communicate through a new language and feel that he belongs to a "wonderful community".

Cameron Jacobs, from Salisbury in Wiltshire, who has autism, ADHD and Tourette's, said joining Orchestras for All seven years ago helped him feel part of a club when many others rejected him.

The 20-year-old, an ambassador for the orchestra, has grown in confidence and has since achieved many other feats, including breaking a world record for being the youngest person to run a marathon barefoot.

Jacobs said: "I feel like music is another language. It feels like you are speaking to people in the audience."

The orchestra aims to help children and teenagers from all backgrounds learn classical music.

'We raised £26k in a week to fight developers'

Dozens of rare heritage sites to open up for free

Before joining Orchestras for All, Jacobs struggled to find a musical setting which made him feel comfortable.

His mum Polly said: "At the time, he had been out of school for nearly a year and it felt like he had faced so much rejection from schools and clubs.

"For the first time [with Orchestras for All] we felt it was somewhere which wanted to accept him with his own uniqueness exactly the way he is.

"I think for any parent looking after a child that has additional needs, there are lot of challenges and life can feel a little bit hopeless sometimes.

Jacobs said when he first joined, he remembers feeling "so excited" that he could just be himself and enjoy the music.

"I feel like I am part of a wonderful community," he added.

"To be part of an orchestra and to play to others, I feel very proud."

Jacobs has also developed leadership skills by becoming an ambassador for the orchestra.

And in 2025, he ran the London Marathon to raise money for Orchestras for All and set a Guinness World Record for being the youngest person, 18, to run barefoot at the event.

A BBC interview after he finished the marathon went viral, with millions watching him hail his mother as an inspiration.

"There is a quote I have held throughout my life and it's, believe you can and you're halfway there," he said.

Nick Thorne, executive director of the orchestra, said Jacobs has become an integral part of the orchestra.

"From a key member of the trumpet section to creating Cam's running, walking and rolling club - a group supporting everyone to be active each morning.

"He's supported many young people to following his own journey of development - and support them all to progress both musically and building key life skills."

Jacobs now has aspirations to work in community music or as a music teacher.

Orchestras for All is performing a free concert in Salisbury at 18:30 BST on Saturday at St Thomas's Church.

articles.title: In 2026, a Florida wildlife centre brought in critically endangered red-ruffed lemurs; the project is now helping restore their disappearing Madagascar rainforest
articles.summary: US News: A wildlife centre in North Florida has welcomed two red-ruffed lemurs, turning encounters with the critically endangered animals into a way to support.
articles.body: A wildlife centre in North Florida has welcomed two red-ruffed lemurs, turning encounters with the critically endangered animals into a way to support rainforest restoration thousands of miles away in Madagascar. The North Florida Wildlife Center in Lloyd, Jefferson County, is now home to four ruffed lemurs. Two of them, newly arrived red-ruffed lemur males, are being gradually introduced to their new surroundings and trained for the centre’s lemur encounter programme, according to WTXL and WCTV. But their role extends beyond educating visitors.The centre says proceeds and support generated through its animal encounters and conservation work help fund habitat restoration in Madagascar, including efforts to plant thousands of trees each year. Its stated goal is to plant more than 1,000 trees annually through its partnership with conservation organisation Green Again Madagascar.From a Florida wildlife centre to a rainforest in MadagascarThe connection may seem unlikely: visitors in rural Florida meet lemurs, while conservationists on the other side of the world work to restore forests.But that link is central to the wildlife centre’s conservation model. Its programmes include a partnership with Green Again Madagascar, which works with Malagasy communities on rainforest restoration, biodiversity protection and livelihoods. The centre says visits, sponsorships and donations help support both the animals in its care and conservation projects in their native habitats.For the newly arrived lemurs, that means their presence in Florida can help draw attention, and funding, to the forests on which their wild counterparts depend.Why the red-ruffed lemur needs the helpThe red-ruffed lemur (Varecia rubra) is found naturally only in northeastern Madagascar, particularly the forests of the Masoala Peninsula. It is classified as Critically Endangered, with habitat loss and hunting among its major threats. The species is especially dependent on intact rainforest. Red-ruffed lemurs spend much of their lives high in the forest canopy and rely heavily on fruit. They also play an ecological role as pollinators, carrying pollen between plants as they feed. That makes the loss of mature rainforest particularly damaging. When forests are cleared or fragmented, the animals lose not only shelter but also the trees and food sources that sustain them.The Florida lemurs are also conservation ambassadorsAt North Florida Wildlife Center, the animals are intended to make that distant conservation crisis more tangible. The educational encounters give visitors an opportunity to learn about red-ruffed and other ruffed lemurs while understanding why protecting their natural habitat matters. The centre also sees the animals as an educational resource for local students, particularly in a rural part of Florida where such wildlife encounters can provide an experience outside the classroom.The new arrivals are still undergoing training and conditioning before they become fully involved in the encounter programme. Their journey, however, represents more than a new attraction. Each encounter offers a chance to connect people in Florida with a forest they may never see, and, ultimately, to help put some of that forest back.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After social media ban for kids under 16, Australia has more bad news for Instagram, Facebook, Snap and online games companies
articles.summary: Tech News News: Following its decision to restrict minors under 16 from accessing social media websites last December, the Australian government is preparing fresh le.
articles.body: Following its decision to restrict minors under 16 from accessing social media websites last December, the Australian government is preparing fresh legislation that would mandate a direct “opt-out” mechanism for algorithmic recommendation systems on digital platforms. Under the upcoming “My Feed, My Way” proposal unveiled by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's administration, tech companies must allow Australian users aged 16 and older to turn off recommendation engines entirely, switching instead to feeds that display only content uploaded by accounts, friends and creators they actively choose to follow.According to a report by CNBC, the measure carries severe financial teeth: social networks, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, interactive gaming platforms and digital services failing to comply could face civil penalties reaching 109.2 million Australian dollars (roughly $79 million).Australia wants to put feed choices directly in user handsThe draft legislation, released on Tuesday (September 8) for closed industry consultation before being brought to Parliament later this year, requires tech firms to actively prompt every account holder with a notification allowing them to select their preferred default interface. Beyond social networks, the proposal orders developers of AI conversational bots and online video games to eliminate addictive interface mechanisms that target underage users.“This is not about giving government control. It’s about giving people control. It’s about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online. This is sensible, pragmatic, practical reform. It gives users choice, and it will hold the big tech companies responsible for inaction,” said Albanese.While major applications currently maintain varying degrees of non-curated views, including TikTok’s “Friends” tab, Instagram’s “Following” and “Favorites” options, Facebook’s personal connection feed, YouTube’s subscriptions tab and Snapchat's split layout, Australia’s law would codify direct, persistent user selection into national statute.Australian government is deepening legal exposure for Big TechAustralia’s regulatory crackdown lands during an era of courtroom defeats and regulatory liabilities for major social media developers worldwide. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a massive lawsuit spearheaded by California alongside dozens of US attorneys general over allegations that Facebook and Instagram misled the public about youth risks.As part of that agreement, Meta promised to introduce chronological feed options, enforce two-hour daily screen limits, and remove cosmetic surgery facial filters for minors within months. The company also wrote an open letter to TikTok and YouTube to follow the suit.Earlier this year, a Los Angeles court handed losses to both YouTube and Meta in a personal injury action that found automated autoplay features and infinite scrolling loops harmed the mental health of a young user.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who directed the nationwide lawsuit against Meta, has also warned that law enforcement officials are now targeting Snapchat, YouTube, and TikTok for similar product safety reviews.Get the latest technology news and updates.
